verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal or the demand, and committers who know the area wrote the series. Four fixable design points remain at level 2. They are the GiST hot standby interlock (replication-ondisk-1), the crash path for table AMs without the batch callbacks (maintenance-fit-1), the lost SP-GiST index-only scans (standards-compat-1) and the changed index tuple counter (standards-compat-2). None of them requires a different proposal.

brief.title: Heap prefetching during plain and index-only index scans
brief.problem: Plain index scans and index-only scans read heap pages one at a time and synchronously, so they cannot use the queue depth of modern storage. Bitmap heap scans already prefetch, but they do not fit queries that need index order, KNN searches on GiST/SP-GiST, or plans where the planner picks an index scan by mistake.
brief.proposed_design: A new amgetbatch interface replaces amgettuple. Index AMs return a batch of matching items per leaf page into a ring buffer owned by the index scan, and heapam feeds future heap blocks to a read stream. nbtree, hash, GiST and SP-GiST adopt amgetbatch, and the series adds read stream changes such as request deduplication and suppression of posix_fadvise under io_method=sync.
user_visible_surface: GUC debug_disable_indexscan_prefetch, a developer option that turns off index scan prefetching (earlier named enable_indexscan_prefetch).
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, IO) shows read stream instrumentation for plain index scans.
GiST and SP-GiST no longer allow index-only scans with ordering operators such as <->, and SP-GiST disables index-only scans for long-value opclasses.
Index AM API: new amgetbatch, amkillitemsbatch, amgettransform callbacks and an amcanmarkpos field; nbtree sets amgettuple to NULL.
Table AM API: new required index_scan_batch_init, index_scan_markpos and index_scan_restrpos callbacks, plus tableam_indexscan.h and batchscan.h helpers.
author_claims: Index scans with prefetching run about as fast as bitmap scans; the first message reports 16 s down to about 1.8 s for 100000 rows.
Range scans on nbtree, GiST and SP-GiST can be 20 to 25 times faster.
The start heuristic, which creates a read stream on the fourth heap block switch, removes the regressions with LIMIT and nestloop joins in the author's microbenchmark suite.
Read stream deduplication turns a 1.15x slowdown into 0.58x of the master runtime on Tomas Vondra's adversarial test.
pgstat_count_index_tuples now counts once per batch, so ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 queries may report many more index tuples.
brief.thread_state: The patch missed Postgres 19, and the slot-based table AM index scan interface was committed in September 2026; v38 carries the remaining patches toward Postgres 20. Open review points are Greg Burd's requests for out-of-core table AMs and Yuhang Qiu's GiST standby cleanup-lock concern; Bilal Kahraman asked whether the SP-GiST INCLUDE fix should be back-patched.
unclear: The material does not say whether out-of-core table AMs without the new batch callbacks remain supported, or how tableam.sgml documents the break.
The material does not show benchmark results for the full v38 series across all index AMs and io_method settings.
The thread does not settle whether index AMs can report recheck per item from nbtree, or a verdict other than dead.
The material does not say how users learn that some GiST and SP-GiST index-only scans are no longer allowed.
The thread does not settle whether the standby cleanup-lock issue is worse with amgetbatch for GiST than on current nbtree.

objections.title: GiST batches on a hot standby can return deleted tuples
objections.failure_scenario: On a hot standby, a cursor runs an index-only scan on a GiST index and holds a batch copied from the root leaf. The primary splits the root, then vacuums the heap and sets all-visible bits. Replay applies this while the cursor still holds the batch, so the cursor resumes, skips heap checks and returns rows already deleted on the primary.
objections.argument: Message #502 reports that the GiST cleanup-lock interlock is enforced only when VACUUM deletes leaf tuples, so the standby has no record that conflicts with the pinned root. Message #507 answers that nbtree has the same bug on master, which does not settle the point. Moving GiST to amgetbatch makes it hold copied items across pins for longer, the same pattern that exposes the bug. The thread summary lists this as an open point.
objections.author_must_show: Which WAL record makes standby replay wait for a GiST scan that still holds a batch from the old root, or why does amgetbatch not make this window wider?

critic.reasoning: Message #507 answers the report in #502 with a question, and the thread shows no reply. The claim that amgetbatch holds copied items for longer has no support in the material and should be dropped; the missing standby interlock stands.

objections.title: Out-of-core table AMs lose btree index scans without the batch callbacks
objections.failure_scenario: An extension table AM that works on Postgres 19 is loaded on Postgres 20. An assert build fails the new GetTableAmRoutine() assertion at load. A release build calls a NULL amgettuple on the first btree scan and crashes.
objections.argument: The brief lists index_scan_batch_init, index_scan_markpos and index_scan_restrpos as new required callbacks, and nbtree sets amgettuple to NULL. Message #515 points out this break, and the thread has no answer yet. The proposal does not say how tableam.sgml documents it, and it has no generic fallback that simple table AMs could use. Each table AM author would then copy the ring-buffer logic, which is the duplication Andres warned about in message #484.
objections.author_must_show: Will a generic batch implementation in tableam_indexscan.c let an existing table AM keep working, and where is the break documented?

critic.reasoning: Message #515 reports that a table AM without the batch callbacks calls a NULL amgettuple in a release build, and the thread has no reply. The helpers added in v27 reduce the duplication concern, but there is no generic fallback or clean error.

objections.title: SP-GiST long-value opclasses lose index-only scans after upgrade
objections.failure_scenario: A site uses an SP-GiST text radix index for index-only prefix lookups on a mostly all-visible table. After upgrade the planner can no longer pick an index-only scan, so every match fetches a heap page. The site finds out when latency rises or EXPLAIN stops showing Index Only Scan, with no warning at upgrade.
objections.argument: Message #491 states this is "a legitimate limitation in the amgetbatch design itself", with no existing bug behind it, and proposes to accept it so SP-GiST can prefetch. That withdraws a working plan type from existing indexes in exchange for a gain on another plan type. The GiST ordered index-only scan removal in message #489 is a bug fix and differs. The SP-GiST loss has no stated user notice: Tomas's documentation patch in message #509 covers only nearest-neighbor ordering.
objections.author_must_show: Which users run index-only scans on SP-GiST long-value opclasses today, and why is keeping amgettuple for those opclasses not viable?

critic.reasoning: Message #491 says the SP-GiST long-value restriction comes from the amgetbatch design and has no bug fix behind it. The thread shows no measurement of the loss and no planned user notice for this case.

objections.title: pg_stat index tuple counters change meaning without user notice
objections.failure_scenario: A monitoring tool alerts on the idx_tup_read to idx_tup_fetch ratio in pg_stat_user_indexes. After upgrade, ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 queries count a whole leaf page of index tuples per call, so the ratio jumps and the alerts fire. The DBA cannot tell a counting change from index bloat.
objections.argument: Message #492 moves pgstat_count_index_tuples to once per batch for a micro-optimization, and message #494 says the change could be "several hundred times more" and "isn't a tiny behavioral change". The argument for it is consistency with bitmap scans, but users have read this counter per plain index scan for many releases. The proposal does not say where monitoring.sgml or the release notes would describe the new meaning.
objections.author_must_show: Could the counter keep its per-tuple meaning at about the same cost, and if not, where is the change documented for monitoring users?

critic.reasoning: Message #494 confirms the counter can rise several hundred times for `ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1` queries. The thread weighed the change and Tomas accepted it in #493, but the visible material names no user-facing note, so the fixable part stands.

refuted.title: Out-of-core table AMs stop working with btree indexes
refuted.failure_scenario: A user upgrades to Postgres 20 with a table AM extension built against the Postgres 19 slot interface. The backend fails the GetTableAmRoutine assertion when the extension loads, or a release build calls the NULL nbtree amgettuple on the first btree scan and crashes. The user finds out at the first index scan after the upgrade.
refuted.argument: Message #515 says v38 sets amgettuple to NULL for nbtree and makes index_scan_batch_init, index_scan_markpos and index_scan_restrpos required. The table AM API was changed in the release before, so extension authors absorb two breaks in a row, and message #486 named that as a reason for caution. The material does not say how tableam.sgml documents the break or whether a generic fallback will exist, and message #515 offers one.
refuted.author_must_show: Will the series include a generic batch implementation or a clear load-time error, so that a table AM without the new callbacks fails cleanly?

critic.reasoning: The slot interface was committed in September 2026 for Postgres 20, so both table AM changes land in one release and no extension was built against a Postgres 19 slot interface. The rest is a duplicate of maintenance-fit-1.

refuted.title: Batch interface leaves no room for per-item recheck or other verdicts
refuted.failure_scenario: A table AM that keeps a row's TID across in-place updates needs nbtree to flag delete-marked entries for recheck. Under v38 the per-item bit has nowhere to go and deadItems can only say "dead". Once amgetbatch ships, adding these answers means a second index AM API change.
refuted.argument: Message #515 shows that xs_recheck must be set for a whole scan, that amgettransform ties recheck to producing xs_hitup, and that the tuple workspace is sized only for index-only scans. The brief lists per-item recheck and non-dead verdicts as unsettled. If amgetbatch replaces amgettuple for all core AMs, its shape fixes what future table AMs can do. It is cheaper to leave room for these answers now than after release.
refuted.author_must_show: Can BatchMatchingItem or the dynamic opaque area carry a per-item recheck bit and a non-dead verdict without a later incompatible API change?

critic.reasoning: The scenario is a later index AM API change, and Postgres routinely changes AM APIs between major versions. No in-core AM needs these answers, and message #515 itself says the extra verdicts need not be in the first commit.

refuted.title: Some GiST and SP-GiST index-only scans are removed permanently
refuted.failure_scenario: A user with an SP-GiST text radix index, or a KNN query on GiST using <->, gets index-only scans on Postgres 19. After upgrade the planner falls back to plain index scans that fetch the heap. The user sees the slowdown in production, with no notice.
refuted.argument: Message #491 calls the SP-GiST long-value restriction "a legitimate limitation in the amgetbatch design itself". It is accepted so that the opclass can get prefetching, and the alternative was "not support SP-GiST at all". The ordering restriction comes from a bug fix (message #489), but the long-value one is a cost of the new interface. The proposal does not say how users learn about either change (brief, unclear items).
refuted.author_must_show: Could long-value SP-GiST opclasses keep amgettuple, and where will release notes or docs tell users about both lost index-only scan cases?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1 for the SP-GiST long-value case. The GiST ordering case comes from a bug fix, and message #510 agrees to document it.

refuted.title: SP-GiST text index-only scans removed to gain prefetching
refuted.failure_scenario: A user runs prefix lookups on an all-visible table with an SP-GiST text_ops index and gets index-only scans today. After upgrading, the planner can no longer choose an index-only scan, so every match fetches heap pages. With a fully cached heap, prefetching gives nothing back, and the user finds out from slower queries after the upgrade.
refuted.argument: Message #491 says index-only scans are disabled for long-value opclasses such as text radix, and that this limitation comes from the amgetbatch design itself, not from a bug fix. The thread shows no measurement of what these users lose, and no field report of SP-GiST heap I/O demand that would justify the trade. Message #491 also says the author would accept leaving SP-GiST out entirely, so a narrower option exists. A committer would likely ask whether this group gains more than it loses.
refuted.author_must_show: What do existing SP-GiST text_ops index-only scan workloads lose in cached and uncached cases, and why not keep SP-GiST on amgettuple until a bounded design exists?

committability.owner_note: The CommitFest entry lists Peter Geoghegan and Tomas Vondra as authors. The owner needs to know nbtree, the index AM and table AM APIs, and the read stream code.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a new index AM and table AM batch interface used by every plain index scan, for its hot standby behaviour, and for read stream changes. This lasts as long as the interface exists.
committability.author_follow_up: Strong sign that the authors stay: the thread runs from 2023 to v38 in 2026 across 17 CommitFests, with regular rebases.

priority.reason: Index scans that read uncached heap pages are common, and message #1 reports about 16 s down to 1.8 s for 100000 rows. The series changes the index AM and table AM APIs and four index AMs, so review and upkeep are costly, but qualified committers are engaged.

precedents_retrieved.title: Index Only Scan for index expressions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch extends the planner so that index-only scans can be used when a query's target list or restriction clauses contain expressions that exactly match index expression columns, not only plain attribute columns. Matching requires the expression tree (or a subtree) to be identical to the index expression; no normalization of commutative or associative operators is attempted.

Robert Haas marked the entry Returned with Feedback because these bugs precluded committing it before the CommitFest ended, while inviting resubmission and saying the effort was good.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

precedents_retrieved.authors: Dmitry Dolgov (erthalion), Thomas Munro (macdice), Jesper Pedersen (jpedersen)

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoid smgrimmedsync() during index build and add unbuffered IO API
precedents_retrieved.summary: Index builds that write outside shared buffers would stop calling smgrimmedsync() at the end and register fsync requests with the checkpointer instead, falling back to an immediate sync only if the redo pointer moved during the build. A new unbuffered IO API (unbuffered_prep/extend/write/finish) would wrap this logic, WAL-logging and checksums for nbtree and other access methods.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The entry was returned with feedback because it waited on the author after review. Andres Freund's March 2022 review asked for API changes, including flag arguments, renamed parameters and functions, documentation and a README update. Heikki Linnakangas then objected that nbtsort.c still chooses between the buffer manager and the new API itself, so every index AM would have to copy that logic, and he proposed a bulk-write API that hides the choice. No new version followed in the visible messages.

I'm surprised by all the changes in nbtsort.c to choose between using
the buffer manager or the new API. I would've expected the new API to

precedents_retrieved.title: Add index scan progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds index vacuum progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum, with counts of indexes to process and indexes processed, including indexes handled by parallel vacuum workers. Later versions keep worker progress in a hash table in the main shared memory segment, so the progress views can read it after a worker exits.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Robert Haas objected to the use of the main shared memory segment and to the locking it adds to progress reporting, which is meant to be low overhead. They asked that workers pass data to the leader through the parallel vacuum's dynamic shared memory, and that the leader report it with the existing progress fields; Masahiko Sawada agreed. Greg Stark returned the patch because of these design changes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
That is, I am imagining that you would want to use DSM to propagate
data from workers back to the leader and then have the leader report
the data using the existing progress-reporting facilities.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add last_vacuum_index_scans in pg_stat_all_tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a last_vacuum_index_scans column to pg_stat_all_tables that shows how many index scans the last vacuum of each table needed. The author meant it as a signal for raising maintenance_work_mem or autovacuum_work_mem.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Alvaro Herrera objected that the column keeps only the last vacuum's value, unlike other stats counters, which are all additive; he and Peter Geoghegan said a history of vacuum runs would be more useful. Fujii Masao asked whether one global counter in a pg_stat_vacuum view would be enough, and Alvaro later doubted the tuning value because autovacuum memory is capped at 1 GB. The author did not resolve these points, and the visible thread ends with a request for a rebased patch that got no reply before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: No other stats counter works that way; they are all additive.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
Reverted commit(s): VACUUM: ignore indexing operations with CONCURRENTLY
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit d9d076222f5b "VACUUM: ignore indexing operations
with CONCURRENTLY".

These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to
miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index
creation.  Before these changes, HOT pruning would have been prevented
by the Xmin of the transaction creating the index, but because this
change was precisely to allow the Xmin to move forward ignoring that
backend, now other backends scanning the table can prune them.  This is
not a problem for VACUUM (which requires a lock that conflicts with a
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation), but HOT-prune can definitely
occur.  In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of
corrupting the resulting index.

Regrettably, this means that the new feature in PG14 that RIC/CIC on
very large tables no longer force VACUUM to retain very old tuples goes
away.  We might try to implement it again in a later release, but for
now the risk of indexes missing tuples is too high and there's no easy
fix.

Backpatch to 14, where this change appeared.

[P9], the earlier asynchronous IO patch set, was returned because it went inactive and its 39 patches were too large to review; this series is split into steps and parts are already committed. Messages #3 and #10 report that 2008-era prefetching work was limited to bitmap heap scans because index-scan block lists were hard to get and OS async IO was brittle; neither was a rejection of the idea.

The GUC is a developer option that does not change query results, and the removal of GiST ordered index-only scans fixes a real bug and has a documentation patch, so neither is raised. The break for out-of-core table AMs belongs to the extension API angle.
The proposal changes no on-disk format, catalog or wire protocol. The concerns from this angle are the hot standby cleanup-lock interlock and the break in the extension API.

The proposal changes how index scans fetch heap pages. It adds no new privilege, role, SQL object or exposure, so ordinary users can do and see nothing they could not before. Batch memory is capped at 128 batches and the dedup cache at 32 blocks, and the I/O depth follows effective_io_concurrency, so an unprivileged user gets no unbounded memory or worker use. The SSI predicate-lock gap (message #500) and the SP-GiST INCLUDE crash (messages #505, #508) were fixed in the series. The GiST standby cleanup-lock issue (messages #502, #507) is a correctness concern for another angle. Without the code, it is not checked that RLS and leakproof quals are still applied after batching in the same order as on master.

Hot-path cost and ownership look addressed. Several committers who know the area (Geoghegan, Freund, Vondra, Munro) are engaged, and regressions were measured in messages #499, #503 and #508. The nbtree VACUUM bookkeeping invariant does not apply, since the series does not change page deletion.

The only existing alternative is the bitmap heap scan, which already prefetches. It cannot return rows in index order or run KNN searches on GiST/SP-GiST, so it cannot do these jobs at all (message #1). No contrib module or extension adds heap prefetching inside plain index scans, and pg_prewarm loads whole relations without scan look-ahead. The read stream work extends the existing read stream mechanism and adds no second one.

Demand for the core feature is well shown. Several independent users and committers asked for it or measured it, an outside workload is described in message #10, and results include about a 10x gain on master workloads and field-style latency tests in message #504. Only the SP-GiST trade-off is questioned.
